video.title: Misconceptions and feedback: Find what pupils really think
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Farah — education lecturer, Bangladesh (main character)
Mr Okafor — Grade 8 science teacher, Nigeria (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: Half my class gave the same wrong answer to the same question. That isn’t carelessness. It’s a misconception: a wrong idea that makes sense to the pupil. Find it, and you can teach straight at it.
Today: the misconceptions every class has, and feedback that helps.
These turn up in every class. One equals sign is the same as two. A variable keeps all its old values. range of one, five counts to five. And the computer knows what I meant.
Three more. Indentation is only for looks. What you type at input is a number. And if day equals Saturday or Sunday checks both days. It doesn’t: or Sunday on its own is always true.

To find misconceptions fast, ask a hinge question: one multiple-choice question at the turning point of a lesson. Each wrong answer is built from a misconception. All pupils answer at once, with fingers or cards, and in thirty seconds you know who believes what.
Read the answers like a doctor reads symptoms. Pupils who chose A think a variable can’t change. Pupils who chose C read the line as text. Group them, and reteach each idea to the pupils who need it.
Quick check! A pupil writes for i in range of one, ten, to print one to ten, and gets one to nine. Which misconception is it?

Off by one: range doesn’t include its end. Don’t just correct the line. Ask the pupil to predict range of one, three, then run it. Seeing two numbers instead of three fixes the idea, not just the program.

Good feedback points to the thinking, not just the error. Instead of: line four is wrong, try: what is total after the first time round? Instead of: you need two equals signs, try: what does one equals sign do?
On written work, give one strength, one question, and one next step. Keep it short enough to act on in the next lesson. Then give time in that lesson to act on it, or the feedback is wasted.
In the app, open Logic gates and pick OR. Flip the switches and fill in the truth table. It shows why or Sunday on its own is always true: OR is on when either side is on.
Your turn. What makes a hinge question useful?

Each wrong answer is a misconception. Remember: misconceptions are wrong ideas that make sense to pupils. Hinge questions find them in thirty seconds. Feedback should ask, and give one next step. And teach at the idea, not just the line.

Try it in class tomorrow: one hinge question. Write a short program and three answers, each from a misconception. Pupils hold up one, two or three fingers at once. Count them, and reteach the biggest group.

checkpoints.prompt: A pupil uses range(1, 10) to print 1 to 10, and gets 1 to 9. Which misconception?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — range stops before its second number: an off-by-one error.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the loop stops one early because range doesn’t include its end.

checkpoints.prompt: What makes a hinge question useful?

options.text: It’s hard, so only the best pupils get it
Each wrong answer shows a particular misconception
It has a trick in the wording

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — then every answer tells you what to reteach, and to whom.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the point is diagnosis: each wrong option is a known misconception.
